tier_reason: README Performance table (MB/s) comes from the public harness bench/compare/run.sh (Makefile target bench-compare, per-library drivers bench/compare/cmp_yam.c, cmp_libyaml.c, cmp_libfyaml.c, shared timing loop cmp_common.h). It runs yam against libyaml 0.2.5 and states compiler (GCC 16.2), flags (-O2) and CPU (Intel Core Ultra 7 155H, one core), so A holds.

corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark from the author's own harness (bench/compare/run.sh), run on one machine and one core; not independently reproduced. libyaml/libfyaml are linked as system-installed libraries (-lyaml/-lfyaml), so their build flags are whatever the distro used. The real-file and scalar-heavy inputs come from rapidyaml's benchmark set and are not bundled; they are passed in through CASES. The C++ rapidyaml event parser is 1.3-1.8x faster than yam on the generated structure-heavy inputs (README's own table). 0 stars; repo created Feb 2026.

notes: All three quoted pairs match the README table exactly: config 206 vs 125, travis.yml 501 vs 149, literal block scalars 3091 vs 290. The README itself states the 1.6-13x range; the 13x is multi-line double-quoted, 3006 vs 224 MB/s. Metadata checks out: MIT, not archived, not a fork, 0 stars, last commit 2026-09-24. The only change is caveats, which now note that rapidyaml leads on the generated inputs.

tier_reason: The only numbers are a first-party chart, docs/Figure_1.png, with values relative to frxml. The harness that produced it is public at commit 06b3b12 (test/src/main.cxx, test/script/main.py), but it states no compiler or CPU and uses only 3 iterations per size, so the tier is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Chart plots parse time relative to frxml (lower = faster), values read from log-scale Figure_1.png: libxml2 is ~1.8-9x slower than frxml (largest at the smallest inputs) and tinyxml2 ~2.6-5x slower. pugixml (~0.8-0.9x, dipping to ~0.4x at ~260-290 KiB) and RapidXML (~0.8-0.95x, ~0.4x at ~260-290 KiB) are FASTER than frxml at nearly all sizes. Memory: frxml allocates less than pugixml, tinyxml2 and libxml2 throughout, but RapidXML allocates less than frxml below ~45 KiB.
corrections.workload: Parses randomly generated XML documents: pugixml-built trees of 50-1000 nodes with random 5-char element names and one attribute each, max depth 300, about 0-330 KiB. Timed with google/benchmark at 3 iterations per size against pugixml, RapidXML, tinyxml2 and libxml2 (DOM parse). Legacy Oct-2024 harness test/src/main.cxx at commit 06b3b12; allocated bytes counted by wrapping malloc.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler unstated; frxml library built with -O3 -march=native (frxml/CMakeLists.txt at commit 06b3b12); pugixml, tinyxml2 and libxml2 come from system packages via find_package, flags unknown
corrections.caveats: The chart shows frxml SLOWER than pugixml and RapidXML, the fast incumbents in this category; it only beats libxml2 and tinyxml2. The numbers exist only as a chart image (Figure_1.png, Oct 2024) from the legacy implementation. The code was rewritten in Aug-Sep 2025 with a new harness (frxml-test/lib/main.cxx, vs pugixml/tinyxml2 on UW XML datasets) that has no published results, yet README still shows the old figure. No compiler or CPU stated; only 3 iterations per size. Limited XML 1.0 support: no DOCTYPE/ENTITY, no entity decoding. The repository is archived.

notes: The record inverted the chart. main.py divides each library's time by frxml's, so pugixml and RapidXML sitting below 1.0 means they beat frxml, and the claim to beat the named baseline pugixml is false. I kept the entry as a downgrade with libxml2 (in the yaml-toml-xml baseline list) as the beaten incumbent. The orchestrator may prefer reject/not-faster, since it loses to pugixml and RapidXML. Metadata is correct: MIT, archived, last commit 2025-09-02, 1 star.

tier_reason: The only number is one sentence in tml-c/README: 'about 5x faster than Libxml2 when parsing the same data'. The repo has no benchmark code (only unit tests in tml-c/tests), no workload, no compiler and no hardware, so this is a first-party number without methodology and stays C.
notes: The claim is quoted accurately. Metadata checks out: MIT, not archived, not a fork, 32 stars, last commit 2013-03-10, so abandoned. The comparison is TML-format data against the equivalent XML (the repo's tml-convert tool uses libxml2), so the evidence is indirect, as the caveats already say.
